d.title: The ANN card, at a glance
d.caption: A fully connected stack: every unit in a layer sees every unit in the one below. That is maximum flexibility and the **weakest possible prior** — nothing about locality, order or sharing — which is why it is the right model for a fixed-size feature vector and the wrong one for an image, a sequence or anything with structure to exploit.

children.label: Shares
children.sub: no weights; every connection is its own

children.label: Right for
children.sub: tabular features, a final classifier head

d.title: The parameter count, and where it goes
d.caption: A dense layer costs inputs × outputs plus one bias per output, so the count is driven by the **widest adjacent pair** — and a flatten in front of it is what makes the number explode. That is the VGG lesson of 2.3 in its simplest form: the layer that touches the flattened image is almost the whole model.

d.title: Diagnosing an MLP
d.caption: Four symptoms with four distinct causes. The first is the one to check before anything else, because an unscaled input makes the loss ill-conditioned and no amount of architecture work will compensate — 1.8's condition-number argument applies directly.
cells: clip, and check the loss's domain

d.title: The CNN card, at a glance
d.caption: Two assumptions, stated: features are **local**, and a feature worth detecting in one place is worth detecting everywhere. Both are true of images and neither is true of a tabular row, which is why a CNN on shuffled columns performs worse than an MLP.

children.label: Wrong for
children.sub: tabular data, where column order is arbitrary

d.title: The parameter count is independent of the input's size
d.caption: This is the property that makes a CNN scale. A kernel's cost is in_channels × out_channels × k², with **no term for height or width** — so the same layer costs the same on a 32×32 image and a 4K one, and only the activation memory grows. Compare the dense equivalent from 2.1: 201 million against 1,792.

d.title: Diagnosing a CNN
d.caption: The third row is the one specific to convolutions and the one most often missed: if the final receptive field is smaller than the object, the network **cannot** see it whatever it learns, and 2.2's recursion is how you find out.

cells.text: the floor in the size formula

cells: compute it (2.2); add stride or dilation

d.title: The knobs, and what each one actually moves
d.caption: Four dials and one rule: change the one whose symptom you have. Padding controls whether the map survives the stack, stride controls how fast it shrinks, and channel width controls capacity — and they interact, which is why changing two at once makes a result uninterpretable.
cells: parameters grow as in x out

d.title: The shape arithmetic, done once
d.caption: Every CNN bug that is not a leak is this table. Work it out for your own stack before training — the cost is two minutes and it catches the mismatch that otherwise appears as a runtime error twelve layers in, or worse, as a silently dropped row and column.

d.title: The RNN card, at a glance
d.caption: One hidden state, updated once per timestep by the same weights. The assumption is that **order matters and recency matters most** — which is true of a signal and false of a set, and the decay that makes recency structural is 3.2's measurement.

children.label: Assumes
children.sub: order; and that recent context dominates

children.label: Shares
children.sub: one weight matrix across all time

d.title: The parameter count, and what is not in it
d.caption: Two matrices and a bias, and — the point — **no term for sequence length**. A ten-step and a ten-thousand-step sequence are processed by the same parameters, which is the weight sharing of 3.1. What does grow with length is the activation memory that BPTT must keep.

d.title: Diagnosing an RNN
d.caption: The first two rows are the course's most-repeated RNN bugs, and both are silent. Padding that is not packed keeps updating the hidden state across fake timesteps (3.11), and `output[:, -1]` then reads those updates rather than the sequence's true end.

d.title: Why the gradient decays, in one line
d.caption: ∂hₜ/∂hₜ₋₁ is Wₕₕ multiplied by the activation's derivative, and tanh's derivative is at most 1 — so the per-step factor is bounded by the largest singular value of Wₕₕ, and the gradient over T steps is that factor to the power T. Below one it vanishes, above one it explodes, and there is no setting that holds it at exactly one for a learned matrix.

d.title: The knobs
d.caption: Hidden size is the capacity dial and the only one with a simple effect. The rest carry caveats that earlier lessons measured — bidirectionality costs causality (3.6), depth multiplies the gradient path, and truncation length bounds what can be **learned** rather than what can be represented (3.2).
cells: state crosses it; gradient does not

d.title: The shapes PyTorch returns, which are not the obvious ones
d.caption: Three conventions that cause most of the indexing bugs. `output` is every timestep's hidden state and `h_n` is only the last; with `batch_first=False` — **the default** — time comes first; and `h_n` is shaped (layers × directions, batch, hidden), so a bidirectional two-layer model returns four slices that must be reshaped before they mean anything.

d.title: When an RNN is still the right choice
d.caption: Transformers displaced RNNs for text and did not displace them everywhere. The cases below are real and recurring, and the first is the strongest: a causal RNN processes one timestep in constant time and memory, which a transformer cannot do without a growing cache.
cells: constant time and memory per step
a transformer's prior is too weak
the state is the summary; update it

d.title: The LSTM card, at a glance
d.caption: The addition to the RNN is a **separate cell state** updated additively and guarded by three gates. That additive path is the gradient highway of 3.4, and it is why the LSTM's learnable range is around a hundred steps rather than twenty.

root.label: LSTM
root.sub: a gated cell beside the hidden state

children.label: Adds
children.sub: cell state c, and forget / input / output gates

children.label: Key equation
children.sub: c = f*c + i*g: additive, so dc/dc = f

d.title: The parameter count, and the formula that is slightly wrong
d.caption: Four gates, four weight sets, so exactly 4× an RNN. The textbook 4h(h+d) under-counts PyTorch's actual total by **2h** — the two separate bias vectors it keeps for cuDNN compatibility, which are mathematically redundant with one another and worth knowing about when you load weights by hand.

d.title: The one that bites: the forget-gate bias
d.caption: PyTorch initialises it near zero, so the gate opens at σ(0) = 0.5 and the cell state is **halved every timestep** before training has learned otherwise — which destroys exactly the long memory the architecture exists to provide, and produced 3.3's LSTM-at-chance result. Setting it to 1 or 2 is one line and it is the first thing to try when an LSTM underperforms an RNN.

nodes.label: First thing to try
nodes.sub: when an LSTM loses to an RNN

d.title: Diagnosing an LSTM
d.caption: Every RNN symptom applies, plus one that is specific: an LSTM that is **worse** than a plain RNN on a long-dependency task is almost always the forget-gate bias rather than anything about the data or the architecture.

d.title: Reading the gates, when you need to
d.caption: The gates are interpretable in a way most internals are not, because each is a number in (0, 1) with a stated job. A forget gate pinned near 1 across a sequence means the cell is holding something; pinned near 0 means it is being cleared every step, which is the failure of section 03 visible directly.

d.title: The GRU card, at a glance
d.caption: Two gates instead of three and **no separate cell state** — one vector carries everything. That is 25% fewer parameters and slightly less expressive gating: it cannot hold something in memory while hiding it from the next layer, because there is no hidden cell to hide it in.

root.label: GRU
root.sub: reset and update gates, one state

d.title: Exactly three quarters of an LSTM, at every size
d.caption: Three gate-sized weight sets against the LSTM's four, so the ratio is **exactly 0.750** — arithmetic, not an empirical observation. Which makes section 03's measurement all the more worth reading, because fewer parameters did not translate into less time.

d.title: The speed claim, measured and contradicted
d.caption: 'GRUs train faster' is correct about arithmetic and **wrong about wall-clock here**: at all three shapes on CPU with torch 2.10 the GRU is slower than the LSTM, by 2.0×, 3.1× and 1.6×. The cause is implementation, not FLOPs — PyTorch's LSTM has a well-optimised fused CPU kernel and the GRU does not. If speed is your reason for choosing an architecture, benchmark it on your own hardware.

d.title: What the coupled gate costs
d.caption: The GRU's single update gate z does two jobs at once: (1−z) decides how much old state to keep and z decides how much new content to admit, so they are **forced to sum to one**. An LSTM's f and i are independent, so it can keep 90% of the cell and admit 90% of the candidate in the same step. In practice this rarely decides a result, which is why both architectures survive.

d.title: The reset gate, which is the part people forget
d.caption: The update gate z gets all the attention; the reset gate r is what lets the candidate **ignore the previous state**. With r near zero the candidate is computed from the input alone, which is how a GRU starts a fresh representation at a sequence boundary — a sentence break, a new session — without needing anything to clear the state for it.

nodes.label: Reset gate r
nodes.sub: applied to h before the candidate

nodes.label: A fresh start, learned
nodes.sub: at a sentence or session boundary

nodes.label: z then decides how much to take

d.caption: Mostly the RNN list, with one GRU-specific entry: there is no forget-gate bias to set, so the 3.3 fix does not apply — which cuts both ways, since it also means a GRU cannot be broken in that particular way.

d.title: Four numbers describe any digital audio
d.caption: Sample rate, bit depth, channels and duration — and every later decision in this module follows from the first two. The sample rate caps the frequencies that can be represented (§02), and the bit depth sets the noise floor (§05).

d.title: Aliasing: the frequency that comes back as a different one
d.caption: Nyquist says a sample rate of f can represent frequencies up to f/2. Anything above that does not disappear — it **folds back** and appears as a lower frequency that was never in the signal, indistinguishable from real content. Which is why resampling without a low-pass filter first corrupts the data rather than merely losing the top end.

nodes.label: A 9 kHz tone, sampled at 16 kHz
Folds back to 7 kHz
nodes.sub: a frequency that was never there

d.title: Log-mel is not a compression scheme
d.caption: The arithmetic comes out **exactly equal**: one minute of 16 kHz 16-bit mono is 1.92 MB, and the same minute as an 80-band log-mel spectrogram at 100 frames per second is also 1.92 MB. Log-mel is a perceptually weighted re-representation — the same quantity of numbers, arranged so the axes correspond to what matters for recognition. The learnability improves enormously; the storage does not change at all.

d.title: What lives where in the spectrum
d.caption: This is why 16 kHz is the speech standard rather than a compromise. Almost all phonetic information sits below 8 kHz, so a 16 kHz rate captures it under Nyquist — and the content above that is mostly fricative energy and air, which helps a listener's sense of quality far more than a recogniser's accuracy.

d.title: Bit depth sets the noise floor
d.caption: Each bit buys about 6 dB of dynamic range, so 16-bit gives roughly 96 dB — far below the quietest sound the quantisation error can hide. That is why 16-bit integer is enough for speech and why the **float conversion matters**: dividing by 32768 to reach [−1, 1] is the convention every model expects, and forgetting it leaves inputs four orders of magnitude too large.

nodes.label: Forget it and inputs are 10^4 too big

d.title: Windowing, and the discontinuity it removes
d.caption: Cutting a frame out of a continuous signal creates a step at each edge, and the FFT reads that step as **broadband energy that is not in the signal** — spectral leakage. Multiplying by a window that tapers to zero at both ends removes the discontinuity, at the cost of attenuating the frame's edges, which is why consecutive frames overlap.

nodes.label: Multiply by a Hann window
nodes.sub: tapers to zero at both ends

nodes.label: Every sample is covered
nodes.sub: by at least one full-weight frame

d.title: The resolution trade-off, which is the uncertainty principle
d.caption: A longer window resolves frequency better and time worse, **exactly in proportion** — the product is fixed and you cannot improve both. 25 ms is the compromise the field settled on for speech, because it is long enough to resolve pitch and formant structure and short enough that a phone does not change much within it.

d.title: The mel scale, and why a linear axis is the wrong one
d.caption: Human pitch perception is roughly **logarithmic**: the step from 100 to 200 Hz sounds like the step from 1,000 to 2,000 Hz, not like the step from 1,000 to 1,100. A linear frequency axis therefore spends most of its resolution where the ear is least sensitive, and the mel scale re-spaces it so equal distances sound equally far apart.

nodes.label: So resolution is wasted high up
nodes.sub: where the ear cannot use it

nodes.label: 80 mel bands replace ~200 bins
nodes.sub: a better axis, not fewer numbers

d.title: The filterbank is a matrix multiply
d.caption: Each mel band is a triangular weighting over the FFT bins, so the whole filterbank is one **(n_mels × n_fft/2) matrix** applied to the power spectrum. That is why it costs nothing and why it is differentiable — which is what let later work replace the fixed triangles with learned filters.

nodes.label: Which later work made learnable
nodes.sub: the triangles were only a prior

d.title: Why the log, and it is two reasons rather than one
d.caption: Loudness perception is logarithmic, so the log axis matches the ear — that is the usual answer and it is only half. The other half is numerical: raw mel energies span many orders of magnitude, which is a terrible input distribution for a network, and the log compresses them into a range a normaliser can work with. And it turns the multiplicative source–filter relationship into an additive one, which is what makes the DCT of 6.3 meaningful.

nodes.label: Which is what lets the DCT separate them

d.title: Why depth destabilises, in one sentence
d.caption: Every layer multiplies, so the network's end-to-end behaviour is a **product of per-layer factors** — and a product of thirty numbers is exquisitely sensitive to whether each is above or below one. At depth 3 a factor of 1.5 is harmless; at depth 30 it is 191,000×. Nothing about this is specific to a given architecture, which is why normalisation, initialisation and residuals all exist to hold that factor at one.

nodes.label: So hold the factor at one

d.title: Sixteen orders of magnitude, from the initialisation alone
d.caption: Same architecture, same input, same depth — only the initialisation **scale** differs, and the output activation norm runs from 1.5e−09 to 5.6e+07. He initialisation, gain √2 for ReLU, lands at 1.935: the near-unity regime where training works. At thirty layers a factor of 1.8 either way is the difference between a model that trains and one that produces `inf` on the first forward pass.

d.title: NaN, and the four places it is actually born
d.caption: A NaN propagates through everything it touches, so by the time the loss shows one the origin is already hidden — which is why the useful move is to find the **first** operation that produced it rather than to inspect the loss. Three of the four sources below are domain errors rather than overflows, and all three are avoidable by construction.

nodes.label: sqrt of a negative
nodes.sub: a variance that went slightly negative

d.title: Unnormalised inputs are an optimisation problem before a modelling one
d.caption: A feature in the tens of thousands beside one in units gives the Hessian eigenvalues differing by the **square** of that ratio — a condition number in the millions. The stable learning rate is set by the largest eigenvalue and progress along the smallest is nil, so the model 'does not converge' and the cause is the units. This is 1.8's argument arriving as a production incident.

d.title: The gradient norm is the one number to log
d.caption: It is a single scalar per step that distinguishes most failures from one another, which no other single quantity does. A loss curve tells you that something is wrong; the gradient norm usually tells you **which** thing — and it costs one line.
cells: clip it; lower the learning rate
the problem is the model or the data

d.title: The loss spike, and what it usually is
d.caption: A sudden spike after stable training is almost never the model and almost always one of three things: a **batch of outliers**, a learning-rate schedule that stepped up, or numerical overflow in reduced precision. The diagnostic that separates them is cheap — log the batch indices, and a spike that recurs at the same data is a data problem.

nodes.label: The schedule stepped up
nodes.sub: a warm restart, or a bug

nodes.label: fp16 overflow
nodes.sub: the scaler should have skipped it

nodes.label: Then clip, or fix the data

d.title: Warmup and decay, and what each half is for
d.caption: They solve different problems. **Warmup** protects the first few hundred steps, when the parameters are random and Adam's second-moment estimate is still unreliable, so a full-size step can move the model somewhere it cannot recover from. **Decay** is for the end, when large steps bounce around the minimum instead of settling into it.

nodes.label: Warmup: ramp the rate up
nodes.sub: a few hundred to a few thousand steps

nodes.label: Large steps bounce at the minimum

d.title: Dead ReLUs, found by measurement rather than suspicion
d.caption: A dead unit outputs zero for every input in the dataset and therefore receives no gradient ever again (1.2). The way to find them is to **count**: hook the activations and report the fraction of units that are zero across a whole epoch. A few per cent is normal sparsity; forty per cent is a learning rate that was too high earlier in training.

nodes.label: Forty per cent: a problem
nodes.sub: the rate was too high earlier

nodes.label: Lower the rate, or warm up

d.title: What to log, and what each line buys
d.caption: Six scalars per step, and together they distinguish nearly every failure in this module from the others. The gradient norm is the highest-value single line (7.1); the learning rate is the one people assume they know and are most often wrong about, because a scheduler bug is invisible in the loss.

d.title: The pre-flight checklist, in the order that fails fastest
d.caption: Each step is cheap and each rules out a class of problem, so the order is by cost: the first four take under a minute together and catch most of what goes wrong. Running them in order means never debugging a distributed job for a bug that a single batch would have exposed.

d.title: Closing the track: what this module leaves you with
d.caption: Three habits rather than three facts. Depth makes everything multiplicative, so the per-layer factor is the quantity to control; a surprising result is a bug report against your own setup until a **discriminating measurement** says otherwise (4.9); and the cheap checks run first, because the expensive ones only make sense once the cheap ones pass.
